lesson.title: Chasing Shadows: Similar Triangles in Motion
lesson.summary: A shadow cast by a light source is governed by similar triangles rather than the Pythagorean theorem, and because that relationship is linear, the shadow's length turns out to grow at a perfectly constant rate no matter how far the person has already walked.
lesson.body:
The shadow problem looks like a distant cousin of the ladder problem, since both involve a right triangle, but the governing relationship is different, and that difference matters. Picture a streetlight mounted at the top of a pole, with a person walking away from the pole along the ground, casting a shadow on the far side. The light ray travels in a straight line from the top of the pole, over the top of the person's head, to the tip of the shadow, and that single straight line creates two similar right triangles: a large one from the base of the pole to the tip of the shadow, and a smaller one from the person to the tip of the shadow.

Let H be the height of the pole (constant), h be the height of the person (constant), x be the distance from the pole to the person (changing as they walk), and s be the length of the shadow, measured from the person to the shadow's tip (also changing). Because the two triangles share the same light ray and the same angle at the ground, they are similar, which gives the proportion H / (x + s) = h / s, where x + s is the total distance from the pole to the tip of the shadow.

Here is the fully worked example. A streetlight is 15 feet high. A 6-foot-tall person walks away from the pole at 5 feet per second. Find the rate at which the length of the person's shadow is growing. Start from the similar triangles relationship: 15 / (x + s) = 6 / s. Cross multiplying gives 15s = 6(x + s) = 6x + 6s, and subtracting 6s from both sides gives 9s = 6x, so s = (2/3) x. This relationship holds at every instant, so it can be differentiated directly with respect to t: ds/dt = (2/3)(dx/dt) = (2/3)(5) = 10/3 feet per second, approximately 3.33 feet per second.

A natural follow-up question is how fast the tip of the shadow itself moves along the ground, which is the sum of both motions, the person walking and the shadow stretching, since the tip's distance from the pole is x + s: d(x+s)/dt = dx/dt + ds/dt = 5 + 10/3 = 25/3 feet per second, about 8.33 feet per second.

The most interesting feature of this problem is what did not happen: the answer ds/dt = 10/3 did not depend on how far the person had already walked, because the relationship s = (2/3) x is linear in x, a direct consequence of similar triangles always producing a fixed ratio between corresponding sides. This is worth contrasting directly with the ladder problem, where x^2 + y^2 = L^2 is not linear, and the descent rate of the ladder's top genuinely depended on how far the base had already slid. Whenever a related rates relationship comes from similar triangles, expect the resulting rate to be constant. Whenever it comes from the Pythagorean theorem or a volume formula, expect the rate to depend on the specific instant.
